title: Train in private
hookLine: train in private: drink water in the heat and tell no one (Discourses 3.12)

lines: A TEST TO TELL THEM APART.
cards: The ice bath video. The five a.m. run, posted at five-oh-two. The green juice and the caption about discipline.
There's a whole economy now of being seen doing hard things. Some of it is genuinely inspiring. Some of it is mostly about being seen.
Epictetus warned about a version of this in his own day, philosophers staging feats of endurance, and he had a test for telling the two apart.

teach.b: Discourses book three, chapter twelve, on training. First he rules things out. Don't train with stunts that are strange or showy, or philosophers will be no different from street performers.
Walking a tightrope is hard and dangerous, but that's no reason to practice it. Train where it's useful: in what you want and what you avoid. Then he gets pointed.

Some philosophers hugged cold statues in winter to show how tough they were; the story is told of the Cynic Diogenes. Don't, he says. If you want to train your endurance, do it for yourself, not for the people watching.

teach.h: A MOUTHFUL OF WATER, SPAT OUT.
teach.b: When you're hot and very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. Notice: you don't even get to swallow it. The water is right there, and you let it go.

A smaller version: if you've given up wine, don't go around announcing, I only drink water. The moment you announce it, part of the training can turn into a performance, and the performance takes the reward.
Training in private keeps the reward in you, getting stronger. Sharing isn't always wrong.

teach.h: WOULD YOU DO IT IF NO ONE KNEW?
teach.b: It's a test: would you still do it if no one ever knew? Look back at the week: show me one, no scorekeeping, real beauty, three fields, found doing this, this too trains.

how: Some Stoic practitioners keep at least one discipline entirely private, following Epictetus' advice to train for themselves rather than for an audience.

o: training, done quietly for your own sake
giving up comforts to win others' praise
a harsh feat of endurance done in public

games.q: train in private: tap the pairs.
p: spit it out, tell no one

s: Epictetus says to train with hard, showy feats
he rules out stunts like tightrope walking and hugging cold statues.
his exercise: when thirsty, take cold water in your mouth, spit it out, tell no one
you don't even swallow it, and you don't mention it.
he says it's always wrong to share anything about your practice
it's a test: would you still do it if no one ever knew?

games.q: you're hot and very thirsty, and you want to train your self-control. what does Epictetus suggest?
o: drink slowly, in public, so people learn from you.
take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.
go without water all day and post about it.
games.why: the exercise is small, real and completely private: the reward stays in you, not in the audience.

practice: Choose one small piece of training no one will ever see: skipping a second helping, an hour without your phone, holding back a complaint. Picture doing it, then picture the urge to mention it afterward, and let that pass too.
Keep it between you and you.

wordCard.voice: Askēsis. Greek for training: Epictetus' rule for practice, no stunts, no announcements; take the cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.

orig.note: Greek askēsis: training, exercise (our word ascetic comes from it); the subject of Discourses 3.12.

carryVoice: Your line: privately. A mouthful of cold water, and no one told. Day four hundred twenty, and a week done.
